cards.front: How do you invoke a static method reflectively?
cards.back: method.invoke(null, args) — the instance argument is null
cards.extra: The receiver slot is ignored for static methods; passing an object instead throws IllegalArgumentException.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection

cards.front: What separates classpath entries?
cards.back: ; on Windows and : on Unix — plus * to match every jar in a directory
cards.extra: The wrong separator silently yields a one-entry classpath pointing at a nonsense path.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Does an abstract class have constructors?
cards.back: Yes — they are called by subclass constructors via super(); they just cannot be called with new
cards.extra: That is how an abstract class initialises the state it shares with its subclasses.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: What does javac --release do that -source and -target do not?
cards.back: It compiles against the API of that release, not just its bytecode version
cards.extra: -source/-target let you call newer library methods that will not exist at run time; --release makes that a compile error.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why can -source 8 -target 8 compile code that fails on Java 8?
cards.back: Because javac still links against the current JDK's own class library
cards.extra: Only --release 8 uses the historical API signatures. That is the option to trust for backward compatibility.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why do field annotations sometimes return nothing at run time?
cards.back: The annotation's retention is not RUNTIME — CLASS or SOURCE annotations are discarded before reflection sees them
cards.extra: That is the usual reason a custom annotation appears to vanish.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::02 Annotations

cards.front: What is package-info.java for?
cards.back: Holding package-level annotations and Javadoc, since a package declaration cannot carry them elsewhere
cards.extra: It is compiled to a synthetic class named package-info.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::19 Packages

cards.front: What is the difference between a static class and a singleton?
cards.back: A static-only class holds no state instance and cannot implement interfaces or be passed around; a singleton is an object
cards.extra: That is why singletons can be mocked and injected while static utilities cannot.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword

cards.front: What is a deserialization gadget chain?
cards.back: A crafted byte stream whose classes, when deserialized, execute code through their own readObject methods
cards.extra: The defence is a serialization filter (JEP 290) or avoiding Java serialization for untrusted input entirely.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization

cards.front: When is a constant inlined into calling code?
cards.back: When it is a static final of a primitive or String type initialised with a constant expression
cards.extra: Changing it later does not affect already-compiled callers — the classic reason to avoid deep dependency on constants.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::04 Static Keyword

cards.front: How do you call a private method reflectively?
cards.back: getDeclaredMethod(...) then setAccessible(true)
cards.extra: Java 9+ modules can refuse this with InaccessibleObjectException unless the package is opened.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection

cards.front: What does Field.setAccessible(true) actually bypass?
cards.back: The access check on that member, not the field's semantics — the value still belongs to the object
cards.extra: Final fields written this way are not guaranteed to be visible to other threads.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection

cards.front: Can an enum extend a class?
cards.back: No — it already extends java.lang.Enum, but it can implement interfaces
cards.extra: Implementing an interface is how you get polymorphic behaviour across enum constants.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::09 Enums

cards.front: What is the difference between Character.isLetter and isAlphabetic?
cards.back: isLetter is the general category L; isAlphabetic adds letter numbers and other alphabetic marks
cards.extra: They disagree for a handful of code points, which matters when validating identifiers.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types

cards.front: What is the @Serial annotation for?
cards.back: It marks serialization members — serialVersionUID, writeObject, readResolve — so the compiler can verify them
cards.extra: A typo in those method names otherwise fails silently at run time.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::17 Serialization

cards.front: Does System.exit run finally blocks?
cards.back: No — it terminates the JVM immediately, though shutdown hooks do run
cards.extra: Any code after it is unreachable; use it at the top level only, in a defined exit path.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Does System.gc() force a collection?
cards.back: No — it is a suggestion the JVM may ignore, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC can make it a no-op
cards.extra: HotSpot performs a full GC by default on the call, which is why production code should not call it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What is the difference between i++ and ++i?
cards.back: Postfix returns the old value then increments; prefix increments then returns the new value
cards.extra: As a statement they are identical; the distinction only matters inside a larger expression.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::03 Data Types

cards.front: What is BiFunction for?
cards.back: A function taking two arguments: apply(T, U) returning R
cards.extra: There is no TriFunction in the JDK — beyond two arguments you define your own functional interface.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: How do you negate a Predicate in Java 11+?
cards.back: Predicate.not(p), or p.negate()
cards.extra: not(p) reads better in a stream chain and works with method references, which negate() cannot.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: How do you combine predicates?
cards.back: p1.and(p2), p1.or(p2), p1.negate() — evaluated left to right, short-circuiting
cards.extra: Composition is why Predicate is a functional interface with defaults rather than a bare lambda type.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: What is currying in Java?
cards.back: Turning a function of several arguments into a chain of single-argument functions: f(a).apply(b)
cards.extra: IntFunction<IntUnaryOperator> add = a -> b -> a + b;. Useful for partial application.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: What are method handles and how do they compare to reflection?
cards.back: Typed, direct references to methods (MethodHandle) that the JIT can inline; reflection is introspective and slower
cards.extra: Handles are checked once at lookup and then invoked like a normal call.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection

cards.front: What are variable handles?
cards.back: Typed references to a field, array element or static variable with defined memory semantics
cards.extra: They are the standard replacement for Unsafe for atomics and volatile access.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How does a dynamic proxy work?
cards.back: A generated class implements the interfaces you list and routes every call to an InvocationHandler
cards.extra: It only works for interfaces — classes need bytecode libraries like CGLIB or ByteBuddy.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::22 Reflection

cards.front: What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?
cards.back: The first is thrown by explicit loading (Class.forName) when the name cannot be found; the second when a class that was present at compile time fails to initialise or link at run time
cards.extra: NoClassDefFoundError often masks a static-initialiser failure whose real cause is elsewhere.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Does values() return a shared array?
cards.back: No — it returns a fresh copy on every call
cards.extra: That is why caching it in a static field is a common optimisation, and why mutating the result never affects the enum.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::09 Enums

cards.front: What does type erasure remove?
cards.back: The type arguments at runtime: List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class
cards.extra: Consequences: no instanceof List<String>, no generic array creation, and overloads that differ only in type arguments clash.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::09 Generics

cards.front: What is a super type token?
cards.back: An anonymous subclass used to capture a generic type: new TypeToken<List<String>>() {}
cards.extra: The type argument survives in the subclass's generic superclass, which erasure does not remove.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::09 Generics

cards.front: Can a constructor declare its own type parameters?
cards.back: Yes — <T> Box(T value), independent of the class's parameters
cards.extra: The type is inferred from the arguments; it is rare but legal.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::09 Generics

cards.front: What is the condition for two axis-aligned rectangles overlapping?
cards.back: They overlap when r1.x < r2.x + r2.w && r2.x < r1.x + r1.w on both axes
cards.extra: Negating it is easier to read: separated means one is entirely left/right/above/below the other.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Do Math.sin and friends take degrees?
cards.back: No — radians. Convert with Math.toRadians(deg)
cards.extra: Passing degrees is the classic silent bug: the result is a plausible-looking wrong number.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: What is the difference between final, finally and finalize?
cards.back: final is a modifier (no reassign/override/extend); finally is a block that always runs; finalize was a GC hook, now deprecated
cards.extra: Three unrelated features whose names collide — a frequent interview trap.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview

cards.front: How do you install a global uncaught exception handler?
cards.back: Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler(...), which catches anything not handled per-thread
cards.extra: It runs on the dying thread, so it can log but not recover; the thread is already terminating.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What are the common causes of memory leaks in Java?
cards.back: Static collections, unremoved listeners, ThreadLocal in pooled threads, and caches without eviction
cards.extra: The objects are still reachable, so the collector is behaving correctly — the reference is the bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Does Java have a sizeof operator?
cards.back: No — only Instrumentation.getObjectSize(obj) in a Java agent, or profiling tools
cards.extra: Object size is an implementation detail: JVM, compressed oops and alignment all change it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: How do you take a screenshot in Java?
cards.back: new Robot().createScreenCapture(rect) returns a BufferedImage
cards.extra: It needs a display; in headless mode it throws. Save with ImageIO.write(img, "png", file).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How do you read and write an image in Java?
cards.back: ImageIO.read(file) → BufferedImage; ImageIO.write(img, "png", file)
cards.extra: The format is chosen by name, and write returns false (not an exception) if no writer supports it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What goes in a JAR manifest for an executable jar?
cards.back: Main-Class plus optional Class-Path for dependencies
cards.extra: The manifest is META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, and every line after the first must be under 72 bytes.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Why prefer ScheduledExecutorService to Timer?
cards.back: Timer runs tasks on a single thread and dies if a task throws; the executor pools and isolates failures
cards.extra: Timer runs every task on one thread, so one uncaught exception cancels the timer for good. A scheduled executor pools threads, isolates failures, and reports them through the Future.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::01 Concurrency

cards.front: How does RMI let you call a remote object?
cards.back: A stub on the client implements the interface and forwards calls to the server's skeleton over the network
cards.extra: It relies on Java serialization, which is why RMI is a classic deserialization attack surface.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What does :: express?
cards.back: A method reference — shorthand for a lambda that forwards to that method
cards.extra: Four kinds: static, bound instance, unbound instance, constructor.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: How do you enable assertions?
cards.back: -ea (or -esa for system classes); they are off by default
cards.extra: Assertions are for internal invariants, not for validating public arguments — a disabled assertion must not break correctness.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview

cards.front: What commonly breaks when migrating to Java 9+?
cards.back: Packages removed from the JDK — JAXB, JAX-WS, CORBA — must become explicit dependencies
cards.extra: The module system also blocks illegal reflective access by default, breaking older libraries.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::04 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Does strictfp still matter?
cards.back: Barely: since Java 17 all floating-point evaluation is strict, so the modifier is redundant
cards.extra: It used to force reproducible IEEE 754 results across platforms.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::00 Overview
